prize_parts.citation: for developing a formal and empirically testable political economics of how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B006 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley. My reasoning has changed in three ways after the exchange. First, I now rest the case on the framework and not on any causal estimate. The contribution is that government became an endogenous actor, with electoral rules, constitutional design, accountability and state capacity as objects of analysis, and with formal models that yield testable predictions about fiscal policy, spending composition and public-goods provision. The constitutional-effects coefficients are the weaker part, and the citation is now worded so that it does not depend on them. Second, I apply the origin-of-ideas test that Krusell and Strömberg use for B001 to my own candidate. It supports Persson and Tabellini as originators of the constitutions and electoral-rules programme. It also supports Besley's state-capacity and political-agency strand, which is a distinct body of work, though partly joint with Persson. Third, I treat the third name as a framing judgement and not as settled. If the Committee frames the discovery around constitutions and electoral rules alone, Persson and Tabellini is the legitimate fallback. The work is 25 to 30 years old and has been extended in many datasets. The 2024 prize answered a causal question about colonial-era institutions and long-run income. This work asks how rules inside a given polity shape policy choices. I regard these as neighbouring discoveries, not the same one. I note that a presentation speech does not establish a private view and may reflect collective drafting, so I do not use my 2024 speech as evidence for the distinction. I rely on the substance. I accept that B001 has the broadest scientific and policy reach on the shortlist, and I do not count it as weak. My preference for B006 rests on cleaner attribution, not on a judgement that its influence is larger.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still identification. Much of the evidence on constitutional and electoral-rule effects rests on observational cross-country variation, and as a builder of comparative regime data I know how sensitive such results are to classification and measurement choices. A prize on this theme must therefore be framed around the framework and not around settled causal effects. The second reservation is the 2024 institutions prize. I think the discovery is distinct, but the Committee could reasonably judge that a neighbouring award so soon looks repetitive, and I cannot show that this view is wrong. The third is that the Besley question depends on framing. If state capacity is not seen as separable, the three-name configuration overstates the credit. A fourth reservation is comparative. B001 is the one entry that every member either prefers or lists as an alternative, and its policy influence is documented in central-bank practice. If the Committee weighs breadth of impact above attribution cleanness, B001 would reasonably lead. I should also guard against my own field proximity, which makes political economics look more natural to me than it may be on common criteria. I considered a two-part configuration. The three-person cap makes any pairing with B006 awkward, since it would reduce each part to one or two names and weaken the B006 credit, so I propose a single part.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and B006 second. He accepts the coherence and maturity of the Persson-Tabellini-Besley trio, but says weaker cross-country identification and the 2024 prize keep it below B001. He names B006 as his first alternative if B001's attribution is judged too diffuse.
responses.response: We agree on the structure of the disagreement. We both treat the identification and 2024 concerns as marginal and not as scientific objections. I would say the identification concern attaches to particular constitutional-effects estimates, not to the framework, and I have reworded the citation accordingly. I disagree that the B001 caveats are marginal. You list a possible shift from Calvo to Galí, Gertler's overlap with B002, priority questions involving Fischer and Phelps, and whether the Taylor rule is science or prescription. These are questions about who is credited, and they go to the choice of laureates. Because your own fallback is B006, I read our positions as close. The remaining difference is whether breadth of policy influence or cleanness of credit should decide. The Committee has to decide that explicitly, and I do not think the exchange has settled it.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first and B006 second. In round 1 he answered Andersson by arguing that Calvo and Taylor originated the pricing and contract mechanisms and that Woodford integrated them. He treats the work of Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets as codifying, estimating and extending that structure and therefore derivative of the discovery being rewarded.
responses.response: I accept the origin-of-ideas criterion as a coherent way to pick three names, and it is the criterion I apply to B006. I would hesitate to call estimation and measurement work derivative in general. In my own field, building the data and measurement that make a theoretical claim testable is often part of the discovery. A criterion that sets estimation aside should be stated openly, and it should be applied the same way to every entry. Applied to B006, it supports Persson and Tabellini as originators of the formal programme and supports Besley's state-capacity strand as separable. It also treats the cross-country estimation as secondary, which is why my citation centres on the framework. I leave the macro substance to you. On that point my view is that the criterion is defensible for B001, but the exclusion of the estimation-side contributors remains a cost of that choice and is not settled by the criterion alone. I also agree that the 2024 prize is not disqualifying, and we both treat the choice between B001 and B006 as a close call.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B006 fourth with Persson and Tabellini only. He calls excluding Besley a hard judgement. He ranks B002 first for the clean Kiyotaki-Moore attribution, and he concedes that identification of the collateral channel is mostly from calibrated or later work by others.
responses.response: I keep Besley, but I accept that your two-person version is the natural fallback if the Committee frames the discovery as constitutions and electoral rules. The question is whether state capacity and political agency are a separate achievement. I think they are, because they rest on their own models and evidence and concern a different margin, namely what a state can do and how accountable it is. Excluding Besley would leave the citation narrower than the work. On B002 I agree about the attribution and the caveat. Kiyotaki and Moore remains my second alternative. I would like macro colleagues to tell us whether any identified evidence, beyond the calibrated quantifications, supports the collateral-feedback claim. I cannot answer that from my own field, and I am not counting it in the mechanism's favour until someone does. Your own ranking of B006 fourth rests on identification and timing, which are the two reservations I have already put against my own case.

responses.point: Strömberg moved from B015 first to B001. He argues that the award rests on originating ideas and not on the forecasting record of DSGE descendants. He treats B006 as a serious alternative with a trio that is arguably cleaner than B001's, though its identification is weaker than that of originating-idea contributions.
responses.response: Your framing of the post-2021 record, that it limits the descendants and not the originating ideas, is the same move I make for B006, where weak cross-country identification limits particular estimates and not the framework. We should apply that move to both entries or to neither. I accept that B006 has weaker identification than the originating-idea contributions in B001. I do not think that makes it the weaker prize on the common criteria. The question is what the committee is rewarding. You note that support counts are not merit, and I agree. The fact that B001 is on every member's list as a preferred part or alternative is evidence that its originators are widely identified. It is not evidence that the contribution is greater, and I do not use it that way.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B006 and argues that Besley's accountability and state-capacity work is a separate strand that links to the long-run historical literature. She says the 2024 prize and this work are neighbours and not substitutes. She also says the citation should be worded around the framework and not around settled causal effects of particular constitutions.
responses.response: I agree on the wording of the citation and have drafted mine on that basis. I also agree that the two programmes are neighbours, though I would not claim that adjacency proves distinctness. The Committee must judge that directly. On Besley I agree with you, with a caution. His link to state-building and long-run historical work is the part closest to my own field, and that closeness could inflate my view of its weight. I therefore rest the case for the third name on independent models and evidence and not on its relevance to my research. I also note that your conflict note records your work with Johannes Lindvall, who is a long-time collaborator of mine. This is a shared acquaintance and not a tie to any candidate, and I disclose it below without adjudicating it.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the 2024 institutions prize as covering this territory or sees the within-polity rules-to-policy programme as a distinct discovery. I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.

Whether the discovery is framed around constitutions and electoral rules (Persson and Tabellini) or also around state capacity and accountability (adding Besley). I think the three-name version is better supported but the framing is a judgement.
How much weight contested cross-country identification should carry against the framework contribution, and whether a citation worded around the framework is enough to answer it.
Whether breadth of policy influence (B001) should outweigh cleanness of attribution (B006 and B002). The exchange has clarified this disagreement, not settled it.

Whether the origin-of-ideas criterion for B001 gives Calvo, Taylor and Woodford or leaves a real case for Galí or Gertler. This is a macro judgement that I cannot adjudicate, and I defer to colleagues who work in that field.
My assessments rest on the supplied evidence and general knowledge. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or the empirical record.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosures, not adjudicated. I have no documented collaboration with Persson, Tabellini or Besley, but I have field proximity to B006 through comparative democratisation, quality of government and state-building, and I have tried to apply the common criteria and not field familiarity. My profile lists co-authored work on corruption with 'Persson' and Rothstein (Governance) without saying which Persson. The chair's summary records this as unresolved. I make no claim that it is Torsten Persson, and I do not rely on it in either direction. Other members note that Torsten Persson has IIES links to several committee members. I am at Stockholm University in a different department from my IIES colleagues, and I have no documented co-authorship with them. I was at Lund from 2006 to 2021, and Kerstin Enflo is at Lund. Johannes Lindvall is a long-time collaborator of mine and has worked with her. I do not have any documented co-authorship with her, and none of this concerns the candidates. My 2024 presentation speech does not establish a private preference.
